messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Cassandra Volk is a 35-year-old single actress who has worked steadily in regional theatre and independent film for over a decade, a career that has always required her to move fluidly through crowded spaces — green rooms, subway platforms, busy streets between auditions. She presented for treatment reporting a PCL-5 score of 49, describing a presentation that had quietly dismantled her professional and personal life over the preceding eighteen months.

The event that precipitated her difficulties occurred on an afternoon commute when Cassandra witnessed a man being violently assaulted on a subway platform by two individuals, one of whom was armed. The assault was prolonged and chaotic. What she recalls is not a coherent scene but a series of sensory fragments — the sound of impact, the colour of the assailant's jacket, the way other passengers pressed back against the tiled wall. She could not intervene, could not speak, and was still standing on the platform when transit police arrived. No arrests were made that day, and as far as Cassandra later discovered, no one was ever charged.

In the weeks that followed, she found she could not construct a reliable account of what had happened. Her memories arrived in disconnected pieces that refused to assemble into sequence — a flash of the victim's face, the metallic smell of the platform, the sound of shoes on concrete — and when she tried to put the experience into words for friends or a brief initial consultation with a counsellor, language simply failed her. This fragmented, nonverbal quality of the memory meant that it never felt finished or past; when it surfaced, it did so with the full weight of the present tense, as though she were still standing on that platform. The reliving experience in turn reinforced her conviction that she remained in danger, that whatever had happened had not truly ended, and this sense of unresolved threat made it harder still to hold the memory at any distance.

What frightened Cassandra most, in the months that accumulated after the assault, was the belief that the world had revealed itself to be a place where violence could occur in full view of witnesses and simply be absorbed — that the people responsible faced no consequences, that the systems she had implicitly trusted had processed the event and moved on while she had not. She had come to understand herself as permanently marked by this, set apart from the people around her who seemed able to ride the subway, pass a uniformed officer, or sit in a restaurant without calculating sight lines. The sense of being an outsider, of inhabiting a different and more dangerous version of the city than everyone else, was not abstract; it was the specific texture of her daily life. These appraisals — that accountability had failed, that she was now permanently different — fed directly into a vigilance that was exhausting to maintain. She scanned every room she entered for the safest seat, always positioning herself with her back to a wall and a clear view of exits. The sight of a police uniform or a visible weapon, even on a security guard outside a theatre, was enough to collapse the distance between present and past and plunge her back into the fragmented sensory world of the platform.

She stopped taking public transport entirely within two months of the assault, rerouting her life around car shares and walking distances that made her rehearsal schedule increasingly difficult to manage. Her director had begun scheduling around her in ways that were noticed by the rest of the cast, and the professional embarrassment compounded her sense of isolation. On the evenings when the vigilance became intolerable, she found herself spending impulsively — clothes, equipment, things she did not need — a behaviour that offered brief relief but left her feeling, in the morning, that she had again done something that separated her further from the stable, functional person she believed others to be. The avoidance and the spending had become their own evidence: each time she rerouted her journey or sat scanning a waiting room, she confirmed to herself that the threat was real and that she alone understood it, tightening the loop between her appraisals and her monitoring until the two were nearly indistinguishable.

Cassandra sought help after a costume fitting during which a prop weapon was left on a table and she left the room abruptly and could not return. She told her intake clinician that she did not expect to feel safe — she had stopped believing that was possible — but she hoped, with some uncertainty, to feel less alone in what she was carrying.
